10226-beautiful-joe-an-autobiography:
Marshall Saunders told this dog's-life story in 1893, with an introduction by Hezekiah Butterworth and a dedication to animal-welfare leader George Thorndike Angell. Joe, a dog cruelly hurt as a pup, narrates his own rescue and later happy home. The book spoke directly to the humane movement of its day.

Early chapters show a cruel milkman, then a kind deliverer and Miss Laura, who give Joe safety and a name. Later scenes praise gentle care and condemn abuse, using Joe's voice to teach children mercy. Readers get a moving, moral animal tale that helped turn many readers against cruelty to animals.
10333-the-european-anarchy:
G. Lowes Dickinson published this study in 1916, arguing that Europe's system of rival states, not one villain alone, led to war. He traces that system from the fifteenth century, through Machiavelli, empire, and the balance of power, to the alliances of 1914. The book was written while the First World War still raged.

Chapters weigh Britain, France, Russia, Austria-Hungary, and Germany in turn, then treat Morocco, the Balkans, the Baghdad Railway, and failed bids for arbitration. Dickinson shows mutual fear feeding arms and distrust. Readers get a calm, critical account of how the old order broke down.
10378-autobiography:
John Stuart Mill published this autobiography after his death, tracing his life from a strict childhood education in 1806 to his later years as a thinker and member of Parliament. Mill's father taught him Greek, Latin, and logic while still a boy, and Mill later questioned that training in a famous mental crisis. The book is frank about both gifts and costs.

Chapters cover youthful propaganda, the Westminster Review, the crisis of 1826, friendship, his father's death, and works like the System of Logic, Political Economy, and On Liberty. Parliament, the American Civil War, and philosophy close the survey. Readers get a classic self-portrait of a Victorian mind.
10960-vergil-a-biography:
Tenney Frank, professor of Latin at Johns Hopkins, wrote this 1922 life of the Roman poet Vergil. Born on the Mantuan plain on October 15, 70 BC, Vergil grew up a farmer's boy in Cisalpine Gaul, studied at Rome. Frank weighs ancient biographies against modern guesses about the poet's family and origins.

Chapters follow Vergil through early poems such as the Culex and Ciris, the Eclogues and Georgics, and finally the Aeneid, with his circle around Maecenas and Augustus in the background. Frank explains how a provincial youth became Rome's national poet. The biography suits readers who know the poems and want the life behind them, set in a clear historical frame.
10986-frederick-douglass-a-biography:
Charles W. Chesnutt wrote this 1899 life of Frederick Douglass for the Beacon biographies of eminent Americans. A chronology opens the book, from Douglass's birth at Tuckahoe, Maryland, in 1817, through Baltimore, the slave-breaker Covey, and his escape on September 3, 1838, to New York and New Bedford.

Chesnutt follows Douglass as lecturer for the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society, editor of the North Star at Rochester, and ally, then critic, of the Garrisonians, who demanded no compromise with slavery. Douglass argued instead for freedom where enslaved people already lived. The biography is concise and admiring, and it introduces a great American life to readers who may know only the Narrative.
11694-the-evolution-of-english-lexicogra:
James A. H. Murray delivered the Romanes Lecture of 1900 at the Sheldonian Theatre, Oxford, on the evolution of English lexicography. He opens in the Commons in 1887, when a member asked for a definition of allotment in a bill, and was told, amid laughter, to look in Johnson's Dictionary.

The humour, Murray says, was lost on the House, since agricultural allotments had no place in Johnson. Later pages trace early word books, from a third part on gods, goddesses, giants, devils, birds, beasts, and wells, to a key for classical allusions in polite literature. The lecture is a history of the dictionary itself.
11962-a-mind-that-found-itself-an-autobi:
Clifford Whittingham Beers's A Mind That Found Itself, an autobiography, went through many editions. The first edition appeared in March 1908, and a fifth edition, revised, in October 1921, with reprints in between. Beers dedicates the book to the memory of his uncle, Samuel Edwin Merwin, and writes from personal experience of mental illness and recovery.

The autobiography describes breakdown, asylum life, and the slow return to health, and it became a founding text of the mental hygiene movement in America. Beers's plain, detailed account argued that the mentally ill deserved humane treatment and organized aftercare. His book helped turn private suffering into a public reform cause.
12085-annie-besant-an-autobiography:
Annie Besant's Autobiography, illustrated and in a second edition, opens with a photograph by H. S. Mendelssohn of Cathcart Road, South Kensington, dated 1885. Besant's preface admits the difficulty of telling a life, still more difficult when the life is one's own. Warns that the telling has, at best, a savour of self-display.

The autobiography follows Besant from marriage and religious doubt through freethought, socialism, and theosophy, to public work that made her famous and controversial. Written by a woman who repeatedly remade her beliefs in public, it remains a candid record of Victorian intellectual restlessness and of a life lived, deliberately, in the open.
12277-the-delectable-duchy:
Q, the pen name of A. T. Quiller-Couch, published The Delectable Duchy in 1906, a book of Cornish short stories and sketches. Q, a Cornishman and Cambridge professor, loved his home county and wrote its people with humor and affection.

Contents include a prologue, The Spinster Maying, Daphnis, When the Sap Rose, The Paupers, Cuckoo Valley Railway, and Legends of St. Piran, with tales of the millstone and the visitation. A mid-book scene watches an old woman in a blue camlet cloak hobble from a grocer shop as trumpets ring out. The stories celebrate village life, dialect, and landscape. The book is a gentle introduction to Cornwall as Q knew it.
12450-the-reason-why:
Elinor Glyn's 1911 novel centres on Francis Markrute, a self-made financier now settled as a naturalised Englishman, and Lord Tancred, an indebted young peer. Tancred, his estates mortgaged and his income thin, talks of leaving for a ranch in Canada. Markrute listens, measures men by use, and keeps his own counsel behind a cigar.

Money, marriage and pride drive the plot that follows, as a bride, a piano-side scene and a husband's jealous watchfulness enter the illustrations. Glyn sets polished London rooms against restless ambition, and asks what a bargain struck for wealth can cost both partners. The title points to that hidden motive, revealed only as the marriage is put under strain.
12549-recollections-of-a-long-life-an-au:
Theodore Ledyard Cuyler's 1902 autobiography, Recollections of a Long Life, ranges from boyhood and college to Britain sixty years ago. Hymn-writers, temperance reform, pulpit work, revivals, authorship and famous people abroad and at home follow. Wordsworth, Dickens, Carlyle, the young Queen, Gladstone, Stanley, Shaftesbury, Irving, Whittier, Webster and Greeley appear in turn.

Cuyler, a Presbyterian minister known for God's Light on Dark Clouds, writes with warmth about preaching, reform and friendship. The Civil War and Lincoln, pastoral work and famous preachers from Binney to Spurgeon complete the picture. The book offers a veteran pastor's view of nineteenth-century America, pious, anecdotal and full of encounters.
12884-reed-anthony-cowman-an-autobiograp:
Andy Adams wrote Reed Anthony, Cowman in 1907 as the life story of a Texas cattleman, drawn from eight years trail driving in the 1880s and 1890s. Reed spends his whole life with cattle, even his Confederate service largely in the commissary department. Apprenticeship, trips to Port Sumner, the panic of 1873, and the Cheyenne and Arapahoe company years follow.

Market scenes give the book its weight: six hundred thousand cattle registered at Abilene, prices holding firm, drovers turning west for winter range. Adams writes with insider knowledge of buying, feeding, and ranch building. The book is a classic of western business life told from the saddle.
12902-a-textbook-of-theosophy:
C. W. Leadbeater's Textbook of Theosophy, published in 1912, offers a clear, simple introduction to a school of philosophy modern culture had lost sight of. Following Sinnett's Occult World of 1881 and Besant's Ancient Wisdom, Leadbeater sets out the Absolute, solar systems, evolution of life, constitution of man, death, reincarnation, and purpose of life. Ten chapters carry the scheme.

A passage on vitality explains that the body needs food, air, and a vital force circulating along nerves like blood through veins, with any blockage harming health. Leadbeater writes for beginners, not initiates. The book is a standard early summary of Theosophical teaching.
13316-the-theological-tractates-and-the-:
Boethius's Theological Tractates and Consolation of Philosophy, in the 1918 Loeb-style edition, pairs Latin with English. Stewart and Rand translate the tractates, while the Consolation uses the 1609 English of I. T., revised by Stewart. The print edition faced Latin and English pages; this text alternates them, with English slightly indented.

Tractates argue over names and persons, asking why God himself should be called Christ, and whether saints might then share the name. The Consolation, written in prison, teaches that power without self-rule is small: though India tremble and Thule obey, black care unmastered leaves might as nothing. The volume is a classic of late Roman thought, philosophy consoling a fallen statesman.
1347-a-new-philosophy:
Édouard Le Roy, a French philosopher and disciple of Henri Bergson, sets out the new philosophy of intuition, duration, and creative freedom that Bergson taught. The book explains how Bergson's thought breaks with mechanism and gives mind and life a central place.

Le Roy writes clearly for general readers, with examples from science and daily life. The volume introduced many English readers to Bergson. It suits readers who want a first guide to a philosophy that shaped early twentieth-century thought. Le Roy's clear guide still opens Bergson to general readers.
13620-the-world-s-greatest-books-volume-:
Volume thirteen of The World's Greatest Books, edited by Arthur Mee and J. A. Hammerton, offers short summaries of great works on religion and philosophy. Augustine's City of God, Calvin's Institutes, the Koran, the Book of the Dead, and the Imitation of Christ sit beside Confucian and Hindu writings, Pascal, Penn, and Paine.

Each entry gives the author's life and the main lines of the work, so a reader can grasp a classic without reading it whole. The Confucian section follows rulers who kept ancestral rites and honoured their forebears, while the Penn section quotes maxims written in prison. The volume was made for general readers who wanted a map of the world's religious thought in one handy book.
13889-dave-ranney-or-thirty-years-on-the:
Dave Ranney told his life story in this 1910 autobiography, with an introduction by Rev. A. F. Schauffler. Ranney spent thirty years on New York's Bowery, in drink, crime, and poverty. He dedicates the book to Schauffler, who stuck by him through thick and thin. A verse by Lucy Whittemore Myrick heads the dedication.

Ranney recalls boyhood flight from his mother's whip and a drunken father at home. Later chapters follow saloons, missions, and slow reform. His tone is frank and penitential, without self-pity. The book offers a rare insider view of Bowery life. It also serves as a temperance and rescue-mission document of its time.
14985-valere-aude-dare-to-be-healthy:
Louis Dechmann, a biologist and chemist of the body, offers Valere Aude, dare to be healthy. It is a short guide on biology and a diet and hygiene method of healing, second edition from Seattle in 1919. Dedicated to the voiceless multitude, the people, it quotes Pope on dispelling cloud and restoring light.

Dechmann addresses suffering humanity, steeped to the lips in affliction, as Longfellow portrayed it, and promises health through diet, hygiene and natural living rather than drugs. His method is now out of date and must not be followed as medical advice. As history, the book shows early twentieth-century health reform: earnest, moral and confident that the body can regenerate itself.
14999-a-briefe-introduction-to-geography:
A Briefe Introduction to Geography, first produced in 1630, only twenty-six years after Cawdrey's first English dictionary and more than a century before Johnson's, keeps strange and variable spelling to modern eyes. Its transcriber notes a small number of absurd cases amended, with all other spelling retained as in the original.

Some punctuation has been corrected, and vowel marks with tilde, implying nasalisation, are shown in brackets. The work teaches geography as it was known in early Stuart England: continents, seas, peoples and wonders in short compass. For modern readers it is both a geography primer and a record of English spelling before it settled.
15697-true-stories-of-history-and-biogra:
A history book for children by Nathaniel Hawthorne, issued in Boston by Ticknor, Reed, and Fields in 1851. Hawthorne frames his tales through Grandfather's chair, an old armchair that has watched history pass. Children gather round as Grandfather tells what the chair has seen. The device lets Hawthorne join separate lives into one family story.

Part One opens with Queen Christina, then moves through the whole history of the chair in three parts. Kings, queens, and colonial figures step forward as Grandfather speaks, each tale short and vivid. Hawthorne keeps the moral plain and the prose musical. The book still works as a first history: true stories told as fireside tales, meant to stir wonder and a love of the past.
15901-a-minniature-ov-inglish-orthoggrap:
A plea for reformed spelling by James Elphinston, dedicated to the Prince and Princess of Wales and the Duke and Duchess of York. Sold in London for one shilling and sixpence, the miniature sets out Elphinston's system in his own new letters. The dedication itself spells English as Inglish, in the reformer's style. Elphinston hoped for universal acceptance.

His system respells words to match sounds, cutting silent letters and odd forms. Royal patrons, he trusts, will lend the scheme weight. The booklet amuses and instructs at once: a serious reform dressed in its own strange clothes. Linguists still cite it as an early, bold try to make English spelling match English speech.
16406-an-introduction-to-philosophy:
George Stuart Fullerton, a Columbia professor, wrote this 1915 introduction to tell students what philosophy covers, how reflective thought differs from common thought and science, and what its main problems are. Chapters move from the meaning of philosophy through the external world, mind, and the great systems, closing with why the study matters to everyone.

Fullerton writes clearly and patiently, with practical advice on spirit and method. The book assumes no prior training, only a willingness to think hard. For beginners, it remains a sane, old-fashioned doorway into philosophy, free of jargon and full of common sense.
16772-the-story-of-a-soul-l-histoire-d-u:
St. Therese of Lisieux wrote this autobiography, here in a translation drawn from the 1912 Burns, Oates and Washbourne edition edited by T. N. Taylor, with a preface by Cardinal Bourne. It holds the autobiography itself plus counsels, letters, and selected poems, with a prologue on her parentage and birth and an epilogue on her final illness and death. Tales of favors and beatification papers are left out.

Therese tells of a small, hidden life lived with great love, in plain, heartfelt prose. Her little way of trust and small deeds has moved millions of readers. The book gives a direct, moving account of a young Carmelite's soul, best read slowly, and it remains a classic of Catholic spiritual writing.
168-the-history-and-practice-of-the-art-:
Henry H. Snelling published this manual in New York in 1849, when photography was barely a decade old. The History and Practice of the Art of Photography teaches the daguerreotype and the photogenic art on metal plates and paper. Woodcut illustrations mark each step.

Snelling covers cameras, chemicals, plates, exposure, and development in plain, practical language. He also sketches the art's short history and its promise for portraits and views. The book served amateurs and professionals learning a new trade. It now reads as a window on photography's dawn. Modern photographers still consult Snelling for the craft's earliest working methods.
16835-an-interpretation-of-rudolf-eucken:
W. Tudor Jones, a pupil of Rudolf Eucken, wrote this 1912 London book to explain his teacher's thought to English readers. Jones opens with a verse from Paul's letter to the Romans, and his preface says Eucken's work now moves minds the world over. Notes point out kin between Eucken and English and German thinkers.

Jones keeps the work expository, aiming to give Eucken's core in simple form, so a reader need not unlearn it when he turns to Eucken's own big books. The theme is a life of spirit over mere flesh and matter. The book suits readers new to Eucken who want a short, clear door into a hard but hopeful philosophy.
17124-atlas-of-ancient-classical-geograp:
Samuel Butler's atlas of the ancient world, edited by Ernest Rhys, gathers maps of Greece, Rome, and their neighbors for students of old texts. An index gives place names with latitude and longitude from Greenwich, while the maps also show the older Ferro lines, a point the editor flags for users. Cross notes link each map number to its index entry.

In this text form the maps come as scanned pages, best read with zoom, since scale shifts with screen size. The value lies in the place lists and the old spellings, from Grote's forms to their common twins. For readers tracing a march, a voyage, or a battle in ancient books, it remains a handy desk aid.
17301-on-with-torchy:
Sewell Ford's 1913 Torchy book follows its slangy hero through seventeen chapters of city scrapes and romance. Torchy chances it for Vee, pulls a sleuth stunt, bugs the system, and breezes by with Peggy, while Ira shows pep and Aunty flags a rosy one. Foster Lincoln's pictures catch Torchy mid-scrimmage, mid-dance, and mid-makeup.

Ford tells the tale in Torchy's own breezy voice, full of period slang and quick jokes. The frontispiece has Vee marveling at Torchy's shoulders, a sign of the book's light romance. Fans of early-1900s humor will enjoy a fast, funny set of adventures from a hero who talks his way through trouble.
17333-wilt-thou-torchy:
Sewell Ford, author of earlier Torchy books, published this collection in New York in 1917, with pictures by Frank Snapp and Arthur William Brown. Torchy, the slangy office boy hero of the series, returns in short episodes. Their titles match his talk: on the way with Cybil, towing Cecil to a smear, handing out a spill, passing the buck with Ham, and following a hunch.

Myra, Rupert, Elmer, and the boss all cross Torchy's path as he talks, bluffs, and blunders his way through office and street life. Ford writes in Torchy's own breezy slang, which gives the stories their period flavour. Readers get light, fast American humour from the 1910s, best enjoyed for its voice and its young hero's cheek.
17778-sir-john-french-an-authentic-biogr:
Cecil Chisholm wrote this life of Field-Marshal Sir John French, printed in London in 1915 with a preface by Sir Evelyn Wood. French, a Kentish Celt and a rebel boy, spent four years in the Navy before he joined the 19th Hussars and rose through the ranks.

Chapters trace him through the Nile expedition, the fight at Abu Klea, the death of Gordon, and a hard desert retreat with thirteen troopers. Chisholm writes as a wartime admirer, keen on pluck and command. The book gives a brisk, first-war portrait of a soldier then in high command, best read with later, cooler histories at hand.
18577-news-from-the-duchy:
A. T. Quiller-Couch, known as Q, gathered these Cornish tales in News from the Duchy. The first part holds stories such as Pipes in Arcady, Our Lady of Gwithian, Pilot Matthey's Christmas, The Three Necklaces, and The Honour of the Ship. The second part adds Ye Sexes, Give Ear and Frenchman's Creek. Quiller-Couch dedicates the book to his friend Austin M. Purves.

The opening tale starts with a pilgrimage to a remote parish church to see a Norman porch, reached by a slow local train through summer meadows. Q writes with local pride, humor, and a love of the Duchy's lanes and shores. The set gives a charming taste of Cornwall in story form.
18788-post-prandial-philosophy:
Grant Allen published these essays at London in 1894 with Chatto and Windus, after-dinner philosophy in the best sense. The lead essay answers a friend who claimed Italian must rule the future, arguing that need, not sentiment, spreads tongues. English, Allen says, grows fastest, swallowing German, Scandinavian, Dutch, and Russian overflow, with Spanish and Russian next, and Chinese, Malay, and Arabic gaining.

Other essays cover aristocracy, science in schooling, scapegoats, American duchesses, whether England is played out, the Celtic fringe, the decline of marriage, and a glimpse of utopia. Allen writes with wit and a Darwinian eye. The book is a lively Victorian miscellany.
19987-chapters-from-my-autobiography:
Mark Twain dictated his Chapters from My Autobiography late in life. He mocks the usual autobiographer in these pages. Conventional memoirists hunt out occasions that flatter them, he observes. In such scenes the author sees his own life reflected in print. Twain instead lets memory wander where it pleases. The chapters ran in the North American Review in 1906 and 1907. They were pieces of a vast dictated life he ordered sealed for a century.

Twain's method was talk: digressive, funny, and suddenly grave. He ranges from boyhood to fame without chronology's permission. The embargo made these chapters feel like messages in a bottle. Much was cut for contemporary feelings, on his design. What remains is the great voice thinking aloud. It is autobiography as performance, vintage Twain.
20007-lord-george-bentinck-a-political-b:
Disraeli wrote Lord George Bentinck as a political biography in 1852. Bentinck had led the Protectionist revolt against Sir Robert Peel. His sudden death in 1848 cut that leadership short. Disraeli recalls how Parliament congratulated itself on Bentinck's devotion. In an instant he was taken from them, he writes. Memory of the past and hope shaped that grief. The biography doubles as Disraeli's own defense.

Bentinck and Disraeli destroyed Peel over the Corn Laws together. The book argues their revolt was principle, not ambition. Racing, Bentinck's other life, gets its chapters too. Disraeli's portrait is warm, partisan, and brilliantly written. Political biography rarely admits its author so fully. This one is half its subject, half Disraeli.
20500-a-short-history-of-greek-philosoph:
A Short History of Greek Philosophy traces Greek thought from its first stirrings to its great schools. It starts with Thales and the thinkers of Ionia. For centuries before the Persian invasions, the book explains, Miletus led the Greek world.

Miletus stood near the centre of the Ionian coasts of Asia Minor. It was perhaps the greatest and wealthiest city of the Greek world, with four fine harbors. From such trading cities came the first questions about nature and the stuff of the world. The history follows those questions through Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle in plain order.
20626-torchy:
Sewell Ford's Torchy, published in 1909, introduces the red-headed office boy whose slangy narration made the series famous. Torchy works the door and the buzzer of a big New York trust company. He tells his own story in the street talk of the day.

This time, Torchy says, he got a bug that the new Octopus Building might have been put up special for him. Anyway, it looked good from the outside, and he blows in through the plate-glass merry-go-round. The arcade is all to the butterscotch, with everything handy. Ford's Torchy stories ran for years in magazines and books.
21624-fifteen-chapters-of-autobiography:
George W. E. Russell, a Liberal politician and writer, tells his own life in Fifteen Chapters of Autobiography. The book first appeared as One Look Back, and Nelson issued this edition. It opens at a wooden temple in Lincoln's Inn Fields, over the spot where his ancestor Lord Russell was beheaded.

Chapters run from beginnings through Harrow and Oxford to London and hospitality. Electioneering, Parliament, politics, and oratory fill the middle of the tale. Literature and service close a life spent near the centre of Victorian public life. Russell writes with warmth and a rich store of anecdotes about the great folk he knew.
21759-kate-coventry-an-autobiography:
Kate Coventry tells her own story in this novel, presented as an autobiography and edited by G. J. Whyte-Melville. It opens on a rainy June morning in London, with Kate fighting tears over a spoiled trip to Ascot. She had ordered a peach-colored mantle and a fine new bonnet for Cup Day. Her Aunt Deborah thinks the outing should be given up.

Kate is quick, frank, and unlike most girls of her circle, or so her aunt says. The tale follows her through family, society, and the excitements of a young woman's season. Horses and the hunting world, Whyte-Melville's own ground, run through her story. Her voice, bright and unbothered, carries the book from the first page.
21882-the-house-of-torchy:
Torchy, the wisecracking New York office boy grown up, takes a wife in Sewell Ford's The House of Torchy, published in 1917. The opening finds Torchy and Vee on a sleigh ride to a hotel register, marriage on his mind. Getting married, he says, is the biggest sporting chance he ever took. The chapters then follow the pair through jobs, friends, and wartime turns.

Vee goes over the top, Torchy gets the call, and the house of Torchy is founded at last. Ford tells it all in Torchy's slang, a Broadway patter that made the series a favorite. Arthur William Brown drew the pictures. It is light American humor of the teens, fast, kind, and full of city talk.
22204-the-making-of-a-novelist-an-experi:
David Christie Murray subtitled The Making of a Novelist an experiment in autobiography. A book in a shop window starts the experiment. Seeing it in Lipscombe's window made Murray younger by twenty years in a minute. A rush of recollections followed, and he resolved then and there to put his memories on paper.

He traces his path from a Midlands childhood to a London career in letters. Apprenticeship, journalism, failure, and success all get honest chapters. Murray asks what makes a novelist: gift, hunger, luck, or grind. The book answers from one life, told plainly. It remains a handy source on the professional writer's world in Victorian England.
22911-where-we-live-a-home-geography:
Emilie V. Jacobs teaches geography from the schoolhouse door in Where We Live, a home geography for young pupils. Her questions start with the building itself. How many kinds of workers did our schoolhouse need before it could rise? Who supplied its stone and slate? Where did its iron, steel, tin, and timber come from?

Lessons grow outward from those familiar things, to town, state, and wider world. The method trusts children to reason from what they can touch. Each answer reveals a chain of workers and materials behind ordinary objects. Books of this kind shaped how American children first pictured their country. Jacobs's version stands out for its patience and its respect for a child's own street.
2317-the-story-of-my-heart-an-autobiogra:
Richard Jefferies, the Wiltshire naturalist, writes a spiritual autobiography unlike any other in The Story of My Heart. Jefferies describes his communion with nature on the Sussex downs, his longing for a fuller life, and his belief in a soul enlarged by sun, earth, and sea. The book is less a life story than a record of intense feeling.

Its prose rises to a pitch of rapture that some readers find overwhelming and others find life-changing. Jefferies influenced nature writers for generations. Anyone drawn to nature mysticism will find this a foundational text.
23395-orthography:
Elmer W. Cavins, teacher of orthography at Illinois State Normal University, wrote this textbook for the seventh and eighth years under the Illinois State Course of Study, with an introduction by Dr. Edwin C. Hewett. A second edition followed in nineteen hundred six, after a first copyright in nineteen hundred four.

Most of the work is word analysis: roots, parts, and spelling rules that teachers, the preface admits, rarely learned well enough to teach without a text. Cavins shows how a root like ann, meaning year, yields annual, anniversary, and annuity, and builds lists teachers can use in class. The book serves as a plain, practical aid for spelling lessons, prized more for use than for style, and a snapshot of how American schools once taught words.
2386-theodore-roosevelt-an-intimate-biog:
William Roscoe Thayer writes an intimate life of Theodore Roosevelt, drawing on friendship and firsthand knowledge. The biography follows Roosevelt from his sickly childhood and Harvard years through ranching, war, and the presidency, stressing his energy, humor, and moral force. Thayer knew his subject, and the portrait is warm.

The book's closeness is both its charm and its limit: it admires more than it criticizes. As a contemporary life, it captures how Roosevelt seemed to his friends. Readers of presidential biography will find a vivid early account. Thayer had known Roosevelt since their Harvard days together.
2431-is-shakespeare-dead-from-my-autobio:
Mark Twain, in chapters drawn from his autobiography, argues the case against Shakespeare's authorship with comic seriousness. Is Shakespeare Dead? weighs the Baconian claim, mocks the experts, and turns the whole question into a meditation on fame, evidence, and human gullibility. Twain's humor carries an argument that scholars still debate.

The book is less about Shakespeare than about how people believe things. Twain's autobiographical voice, digressive and funny, makes it a pleasure. Readers will enjoy a master arguing a lost cause with glee. Twain's argument borrows from the Baconian pamphlets he loved to mock.
25029-sir-walter-ralegh-a-biography:
William Stebbing's biography of Sir Walter Ralegh, published by the Clarendon Press at Oxford in 1899, follows the courtier, seaman, and poet. It moves from genealogy and the search for a career through royal favour, offices, and Virginia to Essex, the Armada, and the Tower. Chapters take up Ralegh as patron, poet, and parliamentarian, with the Revenge, the great carack, and the Islands Voyage among the set pieces. The reissue adds a frontispiece and a list of authorities.

One vivid passage follows the Islands Voyage home. After want of water and tempests, in which Essex's pilot John Davys proved inferior to Ralegh's Broadbent, St. Ives was reached, and Ralegh's return rejoiced Cornwall, alarmed by descents of Spanish caravels. Sir Arthur Gorges told the tale in his 1607 Relation of the Island Voyage. The voyage was Ralegh's last personal adventure at sea for many years.
25110-the-approach-to-philosophy:
Ralph Barton Perry's Approach to Philosophy, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1905, is an introduction to philosophy written for readers with no technical training. Perry, then an assistant professor at Harvard, starts not from abstract systems but from ordinary life. He asks how practical people already form ideas about purposes, values, and the world.

Later chapters bring poetry into the discussion, with Whitman and Shakespeare as examples of thought expressed through art. The book then turns to knowledge, judgment, and logic. The book's aim is modest and clear: to show why philosophy matters to anyone who pauses to ask what their life is for.
25663-printers-marks-a-chapter-in-the-hi:
This chapter in the history of typography treats printers' marks, the devices early printers used to sign their work. Transcribers note that Greek and Hebrew words are transliterated. Older spellings are kept in quotations. Text inside pictures of marks is transcribed with captions naming each printer.

Printers' marks served as trademarks, badges, and claims of craft pride in the age of hand presses. Tracing marks across shops and towns shows how printing spread. It shows how shops competed. It shows how readers learned to trust a mark as a sign of a book's origin and quality.
25864-philosophy-of-osteopathy:
Andrew T. Still, founder of osteopathy and head of its American school at Kirksville, Missouri, sets out his system in this 1899 book. Still says he long held back from writing, judging the science still young, a great unknown sea of which only the shore was known. He took up the pen, he says, when shallow writers began to drag the new art back toward drug systems he had left behind.

The chapters move from first remarks and osteopathic exploration to the head and the body's inner workings. Still treats health as a matter of right structure and free flow, with nerves, blood, and bone in due order. He speaks of magnetic and electric powers in the frame, and of life and motion kept up by forces we barely grasp. The book is his own statement of a healing art he claimed to have found.
25942-the-translations-of-beowulf-a-crit:
Chauncey B. Tinker, in a Yale Studies in English volume, catalogs and judges the translations of Beowulf into English. Appendices cover incomplete translations and paraphrases, works that render selections only, and two books that bear the name Beowulf but are not translations. Notes explain Old English letters unpacked for plain text readers, from vowels with macrons to thorn signs.

Tinker quotes translators defending their craft, among them Cicero's claim to have rendered Demosthenes not as a grammarian but as an orator, aiming to persuade rather than merely convince. Grundtvig, in 1861, speaks of giving his text new clothes, new money, and new language. The book closes with Tinker's own translation, and stands as a scholar's map of Beowulf in English.
26659-the-will-to-believe-and-other-essa:
William James collected these popular-philosophy essays with Longmans, Green, and Company, copyrighted in 1896, first published in February 1897, and reprinted many times through 1912. The essays began as addresses to student clubs at American colleges, later printed in reviews, and James dedicates the volume to his old friend Charles Sanders Peirce. Taken together, he says, they voice a fairly definite philosophic outlook in plain, untechnical language.

James names that attitude radical empiricism. Most assured conclusions about matters of fact are hypotheses liable to modification by future experience. Even monism itself is treated as a hypothesis rather than a dogma. The world, prima facie, is a pluralism, and higher thinking redeems it from that crude form without ever reaching absolute unity. It is James at his most readable, on belief, reason, and the unfinished universe.
2698-a-mortal-antipathy:
Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote this novel around a curious idea: a mortal antipathy, an irrational dread or dislike that shapes a life. The contents move from getting ready and a boat race to a white canoe, a young solitary, and an enigma studied and still at fault.

A record of antipathies, a pansophian society, and a new arrival who interviews a sphinx follow, with Miss Vincent as a medical student. Holmes, doctor and wit, turns a psychological puzzle into a romance of reason. The book charms as a Victorian study of how fear and fancy rule us.
27531-a-manual-of-moral-philosophy:
Andrew P. Peabody, Plummer Professor of Christian Morals at Harvard University, wrote this manual of moral philosophy for colleges and high schools. A. S. Barnes published it in New York and Chicago in 1873.

Chapters move from action and its springs, appetites, desires, and affections, to governing principles and the right. Peabody then treats conscience, law, and Christianity as sources of knowledge about right and wrong. Later chapters take up rights and obligations, motive and habit, prudence toward oneself, and justice toward others. Fortitude and order close the system. The book is a clear nineteenth-century ethics text.
27821-a-history-of-mediaeval-jewish-phil:
Isaac Husik, assistant professor of philosophy at the University of Pennsylvania, published this history with Macmillan in 1916, in conjunction with the Jewish Publication Society of America. It surveys Jewish thinkers from the early Middle Ages to the fifteenth century.

Chapters move from Isaac Israeli and Saadia ben Joseph through Solomon ibn Gabirol, Judah Halevi, Moses Maimonides, Levi ben Gerson, and Joseph Albo. Husik explains how these philosophers joined Greek thought, scripture, and rabbinic tradition, and the book remains a standard English introduction to the field. Husik dedicates the book to Solomon Solis Cohen as a token of gratitude and esteem, and adds a bibliography, notes, and an index.
27882-kos-ciuszko-a-biography:
Monica M. Gardner wrote this biography of Tadeusz Kościuszko, published in London by George Allen and Unwin and in New York by Scribner's in 1920. Gardner dedicates the book to Wiesława Cichowiczówna, upon the national hero of her country.

The preface says an English biography of the Polish patriot needs no justification, naming him among Polish men and women who shed blood and sacrificed happiness for Poland's liberation. The book follows Kościuszko from Polish patriot to American Revolutionary hero and back, in the enthusiastic, well-documented manner of Gardner's Polish studies.
2818-beautiful-joe-an-autobiography:
Marshall Saunders wrote this autobiography of Beautiful Joe, a dog, with an introduction by Hezekiah Butterworth. The book is dedicated to George Thorndike Angell, president of humane societies in Massachusetts and Boston, and of the parent American Band of Mercy.

Joe tells his own story, from cruelty at a farmer's hands to rescue and a loving home. Saunders writes as a plea against animal abuse, in a voice children trust. The book became a classic of humane literature, and it helped change how readers saw the animals beside them. Joe's scars tell his story before his words do.
3175-mark-twain-s-burlesque-autobiograph:
Mark Twain published this double bill in 1871. A burlesque autobiography answers friends who said they would read his life story when they got leisure, and Twain yields at last to what he calls their frenzied demand. The result is a mock life, full of impossible ancestors and grand claims, written to puncture the solemn autobiography form.

First Romance follows it, subtitled an awful, terrible medieval romance. Its chapters promise a secret revealed, festivity and tears, a thickening plot, and a frightful catastrophe. Together the two pieces show young Twain at play: parody as his native mode, and every high form brought low by a joke told straight.
3328-man-and-superman-a-comedy-and-a-phi:
Bernard Shaw dedicates this comedy and philosophy to Arthur Bingham Walkley in an epistle. Walkley once asked why Shaw had not written a Don Juan play, and Shaw answers that the day of reckoning has arrived: here is Walkley's play. Its profits, like its labor, belong to Shaw, he jokes, since he who acts through another acts himself. The quip sets the book's tone.

John Tanner, a revolutionary in spite of himself, flees Ann Whitefield, who pursues him as the Life Force's chosen father for her children. Don Juan in Hell, the dream debate at the play's center, argues Shaw's philosophy outright. Shaw's liveliest plot carries wit, argument, and a superman theory together, without dropping any of them.
3335-theodore-roosevelt-an-autobiography:
Theodore Roosevelt tells his own life in this autobiography, first published in 1913 and reprinted by Scribner in 1920. The contents run from a forward and boyhood and youth through the vigor of life and practical politics. In cowboy land and applied idealism follow, with the New York police and the war of America the unready. The New York governorship and outdoors and indoors carry the story toward the presidency.

Roosevelt writes in his own strenuous voice: sickly boy turned rancher, police reformer, soldier, and president. Roosevelt tells his life at full speed, from a sickly New York childhood to the White House, without a mediator. It remains the best single account of a life lived at full speed, from a New York childhood to the White House.
4212-culture-and-anarchy:
Matthew Arnold's Culture and Anarchy argues that culture, rightly understood, is the pursuit of perfection through learning to know the best that has been thought and said. Disparagers, he writes, make culture's motive mere curiosity, or worse, exclusiveness and vanity.

A culture that plumes itself on a smattering of Greek and Latin, valued as a badge of class, is no true culture at all. Arnold turns from that sham to a larger ideal, where sweetness and light guide social life. Readers who enjoy Victorian argument will find a short classic that still shapes debates about education.
4220-an-autobiography:
Catherine Helen Spence's autobiography traces a life of writing, teaching, and reform in South Australia. The experience of a depopulated province led her to write her first book, Clara Morison, a tale of South Australia during the gold fever.

She entrusted the manuscript to her friend John Taylor, with whom she had just had the only tiff of her life, and who knew her work for the South Australian paper. Spence recalls editors, friends, and causes with plain, lively sense. Readers who enjoy Australian memoirs will find a remarkable woman's own account.
4261-the-complete-essays-of-john-galswor:
John Galsworthy gathered his shorter prose in this volume. It joins two parts of Concerning Life with Studies and Essays and Concerning Letters. Early pieces linger on an inn of tranquillity in the Mediterranean. They cover sheep-shearing, riding in mist, and memories of old places.

Later pieces turn to quality, the grand jury, and the changing face of England. The literary essays include a novelist's allegory and meditations on finality. They include reflections on dislike of things as they are, and pieces on censorship and art. Together they show Galsworthy observant, humane, and doubtful of easy answers.
4269-complete-plays-of-john-galsworthy:
John Galsworthy's complete plays are gathered here in five series plus six short plays. The first series gives The Silver Box, Joy, and Strife. The second adds The Eldest Son, The Little Dream, and Justice. The third brings The Fugitive, The Pigeon, and The Mob.

Later series include A Bit o' Love, The Foundations, and The Skin Game. They include A Family Man, Loyalties, and Windows. Short pieces such as The First and the Last and The Little Man complete the set. The Silver Box opens with a comedy of class and the courts, and the collection shows Galsworthy turning social questions into stage action.
4391-selections-from-the-principles-of-p:
Rene Descartes wrote his Principles of Philosophy in Latin in 1644, and John Veitch, late professor of logic at Glasgow, translated the selections in this volume. The book reprints the publisher's preface and the whole first part, with selections from the second, third, and fourth parts, matching the French edition of Garnier.

An appendix adds part of his answer to the Second Objections, with formal proofs that God exists. The work was translated into French in Descartes' lifetime, with his own care. Readers get the core of Cartesian philosophy: method, mind, matter, and God, in a compact scholarly form.
476-james-nasmyth-engineer-an-autobiogra:
James Nasmyth, the Scottish engineer, tells his own life, from Edinburgh childhood and an artist father to travels in England and Europe, his factory, and his inventions. The steam hammer stands at the centre of his fame. Nasmyth built his Bridgewater foundry into a famous works, supplying engines worldwide.

Nasmyth writes of workshops, engines, and friends with the pride of a maker, then of astronomy after early retirement. The autobiography gives a clear view of Victorian industry from the bench, not the boardroom. His steam hammer, used for forging large ironwork, made his name in engineering history.
5717-bergson-and-his-philosophy:
J Alexander Gunn introduces the life and thought of Henri Bergson, the French philosopher of time, memory, and creative change. Opening chapters trace Bergson from birth and education onward. They follow his teaching at Clermont-Ferrand and his early books on consciousness, matter, and memory. Later he held chairs in Greek and then modern philosophy at the College de France. Later chapters follow his relations with William James and his visits to England and America.

Gunn explains Bergson's key ideas in plain order: lived time differs from clock time, memory shapes the present, and evolution proceeds by creative impulse rather than mechanism alone. Readers new to Bergson get a clear map before tackling his harder books. The volume suits students of philosophy and general readers curious about why Bergson won such wide fame.
6500-the-log-cabin-lady-an-anonymous-aut:
The Log Cabin Lady, an anonymous autobiography, tells a record of conquering self consciousness and fear through mastery of manners and customs. Its author kept the strength and honesty of her pioneer girlhood, adding graciousness and charm that gave her distinction on two continents. The story came after a luncheon at the Colony Club in 1920. There the author had talked about Madame Curie, whose service to humanity was halted by lack of laboratory equipment and radium she discovered.

One guest then asked a question that opened the author's own story. A mid passage finds her on an ocean liner, dresses, velvet cape, satin slippers, and suede packed in a trunk sent to the hold. Cash persuades a steward to produce her trunk so she can dress for dinner. The two weeks her husband gave her held no quiet hours. The book is a pioneer girl's education in the world.
6567-the-adventure-of-living-a-subjectiv:
John St. Loe Strachey, long editor of The Spectator, looks back on his life from 1860 to 1922 in a book he calls subjective on purpose. He opens by breaking both rules he set for himself, one of them not to name his wife, and owns the breach with a dry smile. A quote from Sir Thomas Browne on the wonders within us sets the tone for what follows.

Rather than a flat list of posts and dates, Strachey weighs what his years felt like from inside, with irony and candor about his own aims. Politics, papers, and private life mix as he judges his choices and his times. The Adventure of Living is a frank, literate memoir, more concerned with mind and mood than with mere events.
7544-quotes-and-images-from-the-works-of:
John Galsworthy's novels and plays made him the chronicler of the Forsytes and of English respectability, and this volume collects quotations from his works with images. The entries run from dogs, with rudiments of altruism and a sense of God, to law, which takes a low view of human nature. They reach love, which has no age, no limit, and no death. Each quotation can be traced to its full context.

One thread stands out in the old excerpt: the tragedy of a life that is unlovable, without quite a thick enough skin to be unconscious of it. Not even Fleur loves Soames as he feels he ought to be loved. That simple, uncontrollable tragedy, as the note puts it, is Galsworthy in miniature: an era that canonized hypocrisy, judged through characters who cannot quite see themselves as others see them.
7976-mr-dooley-s-philosophy:
Finley Peter Dunne created Mr Dooley, the Irish-American saloon keeper of Chicago's Bridgeport, whose monologues to his friend Hennessy became famous in the American and English press. Illustrated by F. Opper, this collection gathers those sayings on politics, wealth, war, and human nature, all delivered in Dooley's rich brogue from behind his bar. Dunne dedicates the book to the Hennessys of the world who suffer and are silent.

Dooley's wisdom is comic but sharp: he punctures the powerful with plain talk and finds the joke inside every grand claim. The pieces read like overheard conversation, which is why they travelled so well in newspapers. The book remains a classic of American humour, and a portrait of how immigrants talked back to the country they had joined.
8054-the-bible-king-james-version-book-5:
Paul wrote to Timothy, his own son in the faith, left behind at Ephesus while Paul went into Macedonia. The letter charges Timothy to stop teachers of other doctrines and endless genealogies, and to insist that the aim of commandment is love from a pure heart. It goes on to set out qualifications for overseers and deacons, counsel on widows and elders, warnings about wealth, and a charge to guard the truth entrusted to him.

First Timothy is a pastoral letter, concerned less with theology than with running a church well. Its instructions have shaped church order for centuries, and also sparked debate about roles and authority. In the King James Version, its plain, fatherly tone makes it a useful guide for readers interested in how the early churches organised themselves.
8281-the-world-english-bible-web-1-timot:
Timothy was Paul's young helper in Ephesus, and this letter reads like a mentor's advice to a pastor under strain. Paul, or a writer using his name, tells Timothy to stop false teachers, to choose church leaders of steady character, and to guard the teaching he was given. Rules for prayer, worship, widows, and elders fill the middle chapters.

The letter also warns against love of money, a line quoted ever since, and urges Timothy to fight the good fight and hold fast. Because it speaks to how a congregation should be run, 1 Timothy became a handbook for church order. In plain modern English, its advice stays blunt and practical.
8374-alton-locke-tailor-and-poet-an-auto:
Charles Kingsley wrote Alton Locke as the autobiography of a working tailor who becomes a poet and a Chartist, and the novel became a landmark of social fiction. Alton, a tailor's apprentice in London, discovers poetry, falls in love above his station, and joins the Chartist movement for working men's votes, learning hard lessons about leaders, mobs, and ideals.

Thomas Hughes, author of Tom Brown's School Days, added a prefatory memoir for this new edition. Kingsley, a clergyman and Christian socialist, used the novel to argue for reform without revolution. Readers meet sweatshops, cheap clothes, and the hungry forties, through a hero who writes his way toward understanding.
8842-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
Paul, apostle by the will of God our Saviour and Christ Jesus our hope. Writes in Weymouth's version to Timothy, his own true son in the faith, wishing grace, mercy, and peace. On his journey to Macedonia, Paul begged Timothy to remain in Ephesus to remonstrate with certain persons over erroneous teaching and attention to fables and endless pedigrees. Which lead to controversy rather than to true stewardship for God, which exists only where there is faith. He makes the same request now.

The letter that follows sets out order for worship, qualifications for overseers and deacons, care for widows, and warnings about wealth and false doctrine. Weymouth's modern speech keeps the pastoral instructions direct and practical. Readers get the church's earliest handbook in miniature, and a picture of Paul entrusting a younger leader with a difficult, divided congregation.
8843-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
Paul, apostle by God's will for proclaiming the promise of life in Christ Jesus, writes to Timothy, his dearly loved child, wishing grace, mercy, and peace. He thanks God, served with a pure conscience as his forefathers did, that night and day he remembers Timothy in prayer, mindful of his tears and longing to see him for joy. Timothy's sincere faith, Paul recalls, dwelt first in his grandmother Lois and then in his mother Eunice.

The letter that follows is Paul's farewell charge: guard the treasure, endure hardship like a soldier, preach the word, and keep faith to the end. Weymouth's modern speech gives the short letter an intimate, urgent tone, as of an old man writing to a younger colleague he may not see again. Readers meet the pastoral letters at their most personal, and a portrait of mentorship across generations.
8874-queechy:
Elizabeth Wetherell, pen name of Susan Warner, writes Queechy, a long domestic novel illustrated by Frederic Dielman, opening with a girl pausing on a bridge. Contents promise a curtain rising at Queechy, things looming dimly through smoke, Aunt Miriam, whether a flower can grow in the woods, Queechy at dinner, and the fairy leaving the house. Later chapters follow the fairy and an Englishman, two Bibles in Paris, and very literary scenes.

The heroine, a young woman of feeling and faith, moves from a rural American home to English society and back, learning to judge character, wealth, and religion. Warner's evangelical domestic fiction was hugely popular in its day, and Queechy shows why: earnest heroines, detailed households, and moral trials told at length. Modern readers will find period piety and gender ideals, alongside a storyteller's gift for home life and for a heroine who grows by choosing well.
9304-initiation-into-philosophy:
Émile Faguet, of the French Academy, wrote this initiation into philosophy, translated by Sir Homer Gordon in 1914. Part One treats antiquity, from thinkers before Socrates to the Sophists, those logicians and professors of discussion. Socrates follows, reducing philosophy to morality as the end of all thought. Plato and Aristotle expand the frame.

Plato returns to the universe, politics, and law, while Aristotle brings encyclopaedic learning to morals and logic. Various schools close the ancient survey. Faguet writes clearly for beginners. The book remains a fine first guide to philosophy's founding minds.
a-mortal-antipathy:
Oliver Wendell Holmes frames his novel as a new opening of an old portfolio. His contents list tells the shape of the puzzle. It names the boat-race, the white canoe, and the young solitary. It names the enigma studied, and a record of antipathies. Maurice Kirkwood, a young man of fortune, lives apart because nearness to women makes him ill, a mortal antipathy doctors cannot explain.

A learned society, a Dr. Butts, and a young woman medical student, Euthymia, all study the case. Kirkwood's own story, told late in the book, reveals the childhood shock behind the symptom. Holmes, a doctor as well as a writer, mixes romance with real medical curiosity, and his last novel keeps a gentle, wise tone.
a-new-philosophy:
Edouard Le Roy introduces the philosophy of Henri Bergson to general readers in this short book, translated from the French by Vincent Benson. Le Roy says the work began as two articles in the Revue des Deux Mondes in February 1912. He aims to make Bergson easier to read, not to judge him fully.

Part one lays out Bergson's method: his distrust of stiff concepts, his trust in intuition, and his view of science. Part two covers the self, memory, real duration, freedom, and the vital impulse behind evolution. Long added notes explain hard points such as perception, language, and immediacy. The book served many readers as their first door into Bergson.
an-autobiography:
Catherine Helen Spence's Autobiography tells the life of South Australia's great reformer, from a childhood in Melrose, Scotland, to the eightieth milestone. Her family emigrated when she was fourteen, and she began in Adelaide at seventeen, teaching and writing. The chapters read like a history of the colony's conscience: wards of the state, education, journalism and politics. In London she met John Stuart Mill and George Eliot, and came home with her reformer's charter confirmed.

Her great cause fills the later chapters: effective voting, meaning proportional representation, which she preached for fifty years and saw adopted for Tasmania and South Australian councils. She worked for state children and women's suffrage, and in 1897 became the first woman in Australia to stand as a political candidate. Readers get a reformer's life written as an account of work, plain, proud, and stuffed with the names of everyone who helped.
beautiful-joe-an-autobiography:
Marshall Saunders tells this story in the voice of the dog himself, a brown mongrel who narrates his own life. The preface insists Joe was real: a cruel first master mutilated him, and he was rescued into the happy home the book describes. An introduction by Hezekiah Butterworth presents the tale as the dog's answer to Black Beauty's plea for horses.

Joe's chapters move from the cruel milkman to his deliverer and Miss Laura of the Morris family. The household's pets, a parrot, a cat, and the fox terrier Billy, share the lessons. Stories of trapped animals, a neglected stable, a fire in Fairport, and a Band of Mercy club for children fill out the moral. Saunders wrote the book to teach kindness to animals, and said nearly every incident rested on fact.
bergson-and-his-philosophy: John Alexander Gunn introduces Henri Bergson's philosophy for general readers and students, opening with Bergson's life. Chapters take up the reality of change, perception, memory, the soul and body, true and false time, freedom of the will, evolution and the gospel of intuition. Ethical, political and religious implications follow, with a bibliography guiding readers to Bergson's own writings.
black-hawk-autobiography:
Black Hawk, the Sauk war leader, dictated his autobiography in 1833 through an interpreter. It was the first Native American autobiography published in English. Black Hawk was then a prisoner after the war that bears his name.

He tells of his youth, his wars, and the treaties that stripped the Sauk of their lands. The disputed 1804 treaty, he argues, was never fairly made or understood by his people. His account of the 1832 war gives the conflict from the Native side. Sorrow and defiance run through the whole story, told in his own cadence. An editor named Patterson helped shape the spoken words for print.
carnegie-autobiography:
Andrew Carnegie wrote his autobiography late in life, and it appeared in 1920, a year after his death. The Scottish immigrant had risen from bobbin boy to steel king. Then he gave his fortune away to libraries and learning.

He tells of his poor Dunfermline childhood, the crossing to America, and work as a telegraph boy in Pittsburgh. Railroads, iron, and finally steel built his empire, step by shrewd step. His Gospel of Wealth teaching, that the rich must give back, shapes the later chapters. The book is both a business story and a case for philanthropy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrosian-hym:
Ambrosian hymnography links St. Hilary of Poitiers, dead 367 and named by Isidore of Seville as the first Latin hymn composer, with St. Ambrose, Dreves's Father of Church-song. They stand as Western hymnody's pioneers. Hilary, exiled years in Asia Minor, learned the Eastern Church's Syrian and Greek hymns, but his Liber Hymnorum has perished. Augustine quotes the first three of a group and credits Ambrose's authorship directly, referring also to a fourth.

The Roman Breviary splits one hymn into Martyrs and Apostles pieces, with translations of the others following. The Ambrosian metre differs little from prose rhythm, easy to build and memorize, fitting all subjects, with metric variety in the odd feet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anarchy:
From Greek words meaning without rule, anarchy names the absence of law. As a modern theory it would do away with all existing forms of government. Society would then carry on every function with no controlling or directive authority at all.

Its basis is the claim that every man has a natural right to develop his powers and follow his instincts. The individual, it says, judges his own capacity best, and personal interest rightly understood improves general conditions. Proudhon, called the father of the system, summed it up as anarchy is order and all property is theft. Later writers such as Reclus and Kropotkin gave it scientific shape, while deeds of propaganda by acts, including assassinations and bombings, ran far past what those writers said they meant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-de-mo:
Antoine de Mouchy, also called Demochares, was a French theologian and canonist born in 1494. In 1539 he became rector of the University of Paris, taught at the Sorbonne, and served as canon penitentiary of Noyon. As inquisitor of the faith he used his influence against the Calvinists, and he accompanied Lorraine's cardinal to Trent, where the great church council met.

His own book defended the Mass, printed at Paris in 1562, and he edited the Corpus juris canonici, the great collection of church law. His editions appeared in several sizes and cities, with and without the standard commentary. The entry presents a scholar-administrator who fought the Reformation with law books, teaching, and church office.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arabian-schoo:
The Arabian School of Philosophy traces how Arabs, who before the eighth century voiced religious feeling mainly in mystical poetry and the Koran, changed. After contact with Persia and other civilizations, they took up speculation and science. The Abbasid caliphs, who took the throne about 750, encouraged learning and patronized Syrian and Persian bearers of foreign culture. Foreign ideas soon stirred a twofold movement among followers of Mohammed.

One wing leaned toward heterodoxy, or unorthodox belief. It questioned Koranic authority in rationalist fashion and rejected current anthropomorphism, picturing God in human form, and fatalism, the doctrine that all is fated. Its spokesmen were called Mutazilites, or dissenters. The article follows that rationalist current and its orthodox opponents, showing how Greek philosophy, translated and debated, reshaped Islamic thought and later reached the Latin West.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustin-loui:
Augustin Louis Cauchy was a mathematician born at Paris in 1789 who died at Sceaux in 1857. His father, a learned man, trained him early, and Lagrange, who spotted his talent, steered him to the Ecole Centrale du Pantheon. He entered the Ecole Polytechnique in 1805, then the school of bridges and roads. He served as an engineer on Napoleon's works at Cherbourg. In spare hours he wrote memoirs on polyhedra, symmetrical functions, and a proof of a Fermat theorem that had baffled Gauss and Euler.

Those papers won him a place in the Academy of Sciences and its grand prize for essays on waves. At twenty-two he resigned his engineering post to teach at the Polytechnique. A staunch Bourbon, he followed Charles X into exile after the Revolution of 1830 and taught mathematical physics at Turin. His textbooks on infinitesimal calculus, differential calculus, and geometry show a teacher as prolific as exact.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-austro-hungar:
The Austro-Hungarian Monarchy is a vast survey article on the European monarchy whose lifeline is the Danube, from Engelhartszell near Passau to Orsova. South of the river lie the Austrian Alpine provinces with Carinthia and Carniola, and north of it the Carpathian and Sudetic provinces. The whole covers about 262,577 square miles with about 48,592,000 people, second in population among Europe's political divisions. Its density runs near 185 people to the square mile.

The monarchy joins three blocks. The kingdoms and provinces of the Austrian Parliament hold 26,969,812 people, and the lands of the Hungarian Crown hold 19,985,465. Bosnia and Herzegovina, with 1,737,000 people, is ruled by Austria-Hungary though still Ottoman in theory. Its peoples include Germans, Czechs, Poles, Ruthenians, Slovenes, and Italians in Austria, and Magyars, Rumanians, Germans, Slovaks, Croats, and Serbs in Hungary. The source list shows long treatment of church affairs, from the concordat to theological schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baconian-syst:
The Baconian system takes its name from Francis Bacon, Lord Verulam, statesman and philosopher. He was born on 22 January 1561 and died on 9 April 1626. At thirteen he entered Trinity College, Cambridge, under Whitgift, and soon won repute for learning. There he came to dislike Aristotelian philosophy, not for its author, but for its unfruitfulness.

It served, he said, only for disputations, and bore no works for man's benefit. He kept that mind until his dying day. In 1576 he entered Gray's Inn for law, then joined the French embassy of Sir Amyas Paulet. His father's death in 1579 left him small provision, and he returned to legal study and Parliament. His Essays grew from ten to fifty-eight across their editions, beside the Novum Organum of 1620 and the New Atlantis of 1627.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartholomew-m:
Bartholomew MacCarthy was an Irish scholar and chronologist, born in County Cork in 1843, who died there in 1904. Schooled at Mount Melleray and St Colman's, he studied at Rome and was ordained in 1869. Back in Ireland he taught classics at St Colman's, served as curate at Mitchelstown, Macroom, and Youghal, and became Inniscarra's parish priest in 1895. His scholarship illuminated obscure points of Irish history, ecclesiastical and secular alike.

His most celebrated work, on the Stowe Missal, dates Moelchaich's recension to about 750. It splits the text into an original Mass from at least AD 500 and later Roman additions. His Four Dissertations on the Codex Palatino-Vaticanus studied old Irish meter and synchronisms. Early essays on Irish ecclesiastical fragments appeared in the Irish Ecclesiastical Record from 1864. A sharp 1897 letter against a review of Salmon's Ancient Irish Church sparked a learned controversy the next year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-biblical-geog:
Biblical geography, the lands and places of the Bible, receives a very long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Almost every Bible book touches the Holy Land's geography, yet early readers inside Palestine needed no guide, while Jews of the Diaspora and later outsiders did. The study grew with the search for the literal and historical sense of Scripture.

Genesis 10's list of peoples, the wilderness journey stations, and the tribal allotments supply its chief materials. The entry surveys sources, maps, and disputed sites, from Dan to Beersheba and beyond. It presents geography as a handmaid of reading the Bible in its own country.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-ico:
An entry on Christian iconography, the science describing, tracing, and interpreting the traditional images in art: God, the saints, and further sacred subjects. From the first centuries the Church used art to teach and edify, painting and mosaicking catacomb walls. It then lent church walls, ceilings, windows, altars, furniture, vessels, and books to scenes from both Testaments, saints' lives and legends, and even old myths reshaped to Christian teaching.

Iconography gives the history of these images, notes where and when each flourished or vanished, compares lands and periods, explains personal and historical details, and reads their symbols. Studied this way, images carry historical and doctrinal weight, attesting the unity of tradition and the faith of their ages. Detail lives in companion articles on diptychs, ivories, metalwork, mosaics, painting, reliquaries, sculpture, windows, and wood-carving.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cynic-school-:
A philosophy entry presents the Cynic School, founded at Athens around 400 BC and lasting until around 200 BC. It grew from Socrates' teaching on moderation and self-denial, joined to the dialectical methods of the Eleatics and Sophists. Both strains were bent from their first uses: Socratic ethics hardened into coarse contempt for knowledge, refinement, and common decency.

Their name, dogs, is often traced to that contempt, though some derive it from Cynosarges, the gymnasium where they met. Antisthenes, a pupil of Socrates born about 436 BC, founded the school, and Diogenes of Sinope became its best-known follower. In knowledge Antisthenes held that only sense-perceived individuals exist, and in ethics that virtue alone is good while pleasure is always evil. His severity lived on in Stoicism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cyrenaic-scho:
A philosophy entry presents the Cyrenaic School, named for Cyrene, where it was founded, flourishing from about 400 to about 300 BC. Its distinctive tenet was hedonism, the teaching that pleasure stands as the highest good. It drew from Socrates, by twisting his teaching that happiness is the chief good into the supremacy of pleasure, and from Protagoras, whose relativism it adopted.

Aristippus, active about 400 BC, founded the school, counting his daughter Arete and grandson Aristippus the Younger among followers. The Cyrenaics held that all knowledge is relative: only our feelings, the impressions things make on us, can be known. Applied to conduct, this meant happiness comes from gaining pleasurable feelings and avoiding painful ones. Virtue counts only as a means to pleasure, and later Cyrenaics merged with the Epicureans.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dennis-floren:
A life of Dennis Florence MacCarthy, an Irish poet born in Dublin in 1817 who died at Blackrock in 1882. A learned priest who had lived in Spain gave him the Spanish that shaped his career. Verses in the Dublin Satirist came before he was seventeen, and patriotic poems under the name Desmond filled the Nation from 1842.

Called to the Irish bar in 1846, he never practised, turning instead to editing Irish poetry and ballads. His own Ballads, Poems, and Lyrics appeared in 1850, but Calderón, the Spanish Shakespeare, claimed most of his later labour. Volumes of Calderón translations followed in 1853, 1861, 1867, 1870, and 1873, with a last version finished only months before his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eparchy:
An eparchy was first a division of the Roman Empire, and this entry traces how the word passed into church use. Under Diocletian and Maximian the empire was split into four great prefectures, Gaul, Italy, Illyricum, and the East, each cut into civil dioceses and then into eparchies under governors. The Church took over this handy map for her own order.

Gaul, Italy, and Illyricum formed the Roman patriarchate, while the prefecture of the East was shared in the fourth century between Alexandria and Antioch and three exarchs. Below patriarchs and exarchs stood eparchies under metropolitans, with city bishops beneath them, and Nicaea in 325 confirmed that the metropolitan in each eparchy should appoint bishops. Later, in Eastern Christendom, the word came to mean simply a bishop's diocese, and in Russia, where it is the usual term, the Church now counts eighty-six eparchies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hagiography:
Hagiography names the study of the saints and their worship. This long entry maps both the writings worship produced and the study that sifts them. Practical hagiography covers martyrologies, calendars, passions, lives, and liturgical texts, from the Passion of the Scillitan Martyrs and Sulpicius Severus's Life of St. Martin to the great medieval legend books.

Critical hagiography weighs those documents for truth, tracing collections from Eusebius through Gregory of Tours and Gregory the Great to the Golden Legend of Jacobus de Voragine, the most famous of all. The line runs on to Lipomano, Surius, and the Bollandists. Readers learn how monographs became calendar-ordered legend books, how condensed lives spread in plain speech, and why each text needs its own kind of scrutiny.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heptarchy:
Heptarchy denotes the seven kingdoms into which Anglo-Saxon Britain was roughly divided for nearly three centuries, until Wessex gained definite supremacy about 829. The term dates from the sixteenth century and appears in Camden's Britannia. Critics object that it should strictly mean seven rulers, and that England often had more or fewer than seven independent kingdoms at once. Stubbs and other modern historians retain it for its obvious convenience.

The seven kingdoms were Wessex, Sussex, Kent, Essex, East Anglia, Mercia, and Northumbria, with Deira and Bernicia often counted separately within the last. War and subjugation were constant between them, and smaller rulers also bore the title of king, as in Sussex, Essex, the Hwicce, and Lindsey. The kingdoms also formed the earliest units of church organization, Kent first accepting the Gospel, with Augustine consecrating bishops at Rochester, Canterbury, and London before his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hierarchy:
Hierarchy, from the Greek for sacred rule, denotes the whole body of ruling powers in the church. The word gained its fixed sense from Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite in the sixth century, who used it in his works on the celestial hierarchy and the ecclesiastical hierarchy. For him and his commentators Pachymeres and Maximus, it meant the care and control of holy things, the sacred principate.

A hierarch, in this account, both obeys and commands, yet never obeys those it commands, so gradation is built into the idea. That gradation exists even among the angels in the heavenly hierarchy, on which the church hierarchy is modelled. It must hold all the more in a human assembly prone to sin, where ordered ranks work for peace and harmony. The entry sets out grades that guide people toward their eternal salvation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ionian-school:
Greek philosophy begins at Miletus, this entry argues. There the Ionian school arose in the sixth century before Christ. Its later revisers followed a hundred years on. Aristotle called its founders the first students of nature, since they confined inquiry to the origin and laws of the physical world. All of them sought one primitive stuff that was both the matter of the world and the force shaping it.

Thales named that stuff water, Anaximander called it the boundless, and Anaximenes offered his own answer, while the later Ionians reshaped those first guesses. The entry separates earlier from later thinkers and shows how a question about what the world is made of became the first philosophy. Readers meet the founders not as names in a list but as rivals over one bold idea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-mullanph:
John Mullanphy was an Irish immigrant merchant whose fortune built Catholic St. Louis. Born near Enniskillen in 1758, he served in the Irish Brigade in France until the Revolution drove him home. He emigrated to Philadelphia in 1792 with wife and child and traded at Baltimore and Frankfort, Kentucky. He settled finally at Saint Louis in 1804, investing business profits in real estate.

He defended Baltimore in the War of 1812, stood with Jackson at New Orleans in 1815, and bought cotton cheap to sell at immense profit when peace came. Father of fifteen children, he spent his last years giving his fortune away. His gifts included the Sacred Heart convent in 1827 and a hospital for the Sisters of Charity in 1828. They also included a church, a Jesuit novitiate, and a Loretto convent, with twenty-five thousand dollars left for education and charity. His hospital and orphan asylum still bear his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-justin-mccart:
Justin McCarthy was an Irish politician, journalist, novelist, and historian whose courtesy won cross-party respect. Born at Cork in 1830, he joined the Cork Examiner at eighteen and later reported for the London Morning Star, which he edited from 1864 to 1868. He lectured across the United States, helped edit the New York Independent, and wrote leaders for the London Daily News. From 1879 to 1896 he sat in Parliament for County Longford, Derry City, and North Longford.

He joined the Irish Land League in 1880, chaired the National Land and Labour League, and led the Irish Parliamentary Party from 1890 to 1896 after Parnell. Yet letters interested him more than politics. His novels began with The Waterdale Neighbours in 1867 and ran to about twenty titles, but his fame rests on the seven-volume History of Our Own Times. Those histories stand out as lucid, forceful, and remarkably free from party spirit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-neo-pythagore:
Neo-Pythagorean philosophy revived the ethico-religious society founded by Pythagoras. That society had flourished in Magna Graecia in the fifth century BC and vanished from history in the fourth, when Athenian philosophy reached its zenith. Here and there a philosopher returned to the Pythagorean doctrine of numbers, with the school's bent toward religious ethics and ascetic practice.

From the middle of the first century BC, a more systematic attempt restored Pythagorean speculative philosophy, joined with astrology and sorcery. Its first systematic figure was Figulus, a Roman at Alexandria about mid-first century BC and a friend of Cicero, with Vatinius and the Sextians contributing. At Alexandria the school's most influential teachers worked. In the second and third centuries its philosophers travelled the empire as apostles of the cult, including Moderatus of Gades, Apollonius of Tyana, Nicomachus of Gerasa, Numenius and Philostratus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-tuit:
Dublin-born preacher Nicholas Tuite MacCarthy, known as the Abbé de Lévignac, rose to fame in France after a late start in the priesthood. Born in 1769 and raised at Toulouse, he left Paris during the Revolution and was not ordained until 1814, when he was forty-five.

Refusing the bishopric of Montauban in 1817, he joined the Jesuits the next year and preached before the French court during his novitiate. His sermons drew wide praise, and he kept preaching across France until his death at Annecy in 1833. Toulouse saw his first missionary labours, and Paris heard him preach before the court.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-palaeography:
Palaeography, from Greek words for ancient writing, is the art of reading old handwriting in manuscripts and diplomas. It differs from epigraphy, which reads carved inscriptions, and from diplomatics, which weighs a document's inner character. Palaeography cares only for written characters and for sorting documents by their outward marks.

Renaissance printing spread manuscript reading, but only in the seventeenth century did scholars turn notes into system. Mabillon's De re diplomatica of 1681 studied Latin scripts with plates, and Montfaucon's Greek Palaeography of 1708 coined the word and the science. French, English, and German scholars then made it the base of all study of old texts. Later pages sort scripts, abbreviations, and punctuation marks across centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-gandolp:
Peter Gandolphy was a London Jesuit preacher whose hasty pen brought him into public trouble. Born in 1779 to a Genoese-descended family, he studied at Liège and Stonyhurst, taught humanities there in 1801, and was ordained about 1804. At the Spanish chapel in London he won fame as a preacher and converted many Protestants, but his methods soon drew censure from his bishop, Poynter.
